doc.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024

title: How he got the Miles Davis job
summary: A friend at Blue Note passed his tape to Tommy LiPuma, Miles said he had the job; first meeting at Miles's door.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Did you have rehearsals for that, was it six or seven weeks that you played with them — at least from what I read — and were there rehearsals before that? Because he’s not calling tunes like “Green Dolphin Street.”

No there wasn’t. And I can tell you quickly the story of how I got the gig is I was living in New Orleans at the time and my friend from high school and college, his name is Matt Pearson who is a producer now, he was working as an intern at Blue Note. And he said, “Put together a demo tape because I can get it to Bruce Lundvall who is the president of Blue Note, and we might be able to do a record together. So I sent a tape and he played it for Bruce and Bruce said yeah, let’s do the record with him. But Matt also sent that same tape to Tommy LiPuma who was producing “Amandla” at the time. And some weeks later I was still living in New Orleans and I got a call from Tommy saying, “Rick, I just heard the tape and I played it for Miles over the phone and Miles told me to call you and tell you you have a job.”

So yeah, that was like extraordinary of course, one of the most extraordinary moments of my life just to have that happen. And of course the tape was good and I had to be able to deliver, but it was also a case of who you know. Because if it wasn’t for Matt being in New York at that time and knowing that Miles was in the studio and like all the coincidences that had to happen for that to happen was pretty amazing. So the original thing was, it was two saxophones. It was me with Kenny Garrett. And I had seen that band and that show a couple of times. So at that point in Miles’ career it was kind of like the same structure every night. There wasn’t too many variations. So I kind of knew what the show was about. So I flew to New York and, yeah, Tommy said Miles wants to meet me. So of course I was scared shitless. It’s like, and I have no memory of getting in an airplane, of flying to New York, I don’t remember how I got in the city, like it’s really strange. I don’t remember any of that. I just remember ending up at the Essex House, the

Marriott on Central Park South, which is where Miles was living, and got to his door and it said “Please take off your shoes.” So I was standing there with my horn and my shoes for about 15 minutes, and I finally got the courage to knock on the door. And he opened the door with a smile on his face and he brought me in and I was totally at ease. It was really, really an extraordinary moment. Because I wasn’t sure if he was going to ask me to play or what it was going to be like. And all he did was he said sit down, and he went on his desk, or this big dining room table, and was searching through a bunch of tapes and papers, and he just gave me a cassette and he said, “I’ll see you on stage.”
